Stephen Marshall
MAR-shul
proper noun
From the surname Marshall; the great preacher of the Long Parliament and a divine of the Westminster Assembly.

Biblical Definition

Stephen Marshall was among the most influential preachers of his age, a divine of the Westminster Assembly and the foremost pulpit voice before the Long Parliament in the years of the civil war. His sermon Meroz Cursed, preached again and again before the Parliament and the armies, took up the angel’s word in the song of Deborah, Curse ye Meroz, because they came not to the help of the LORD against the mighty (Jdg 5:23), to rouse a slumbering people to the cause of reformation. He was one of the five authors of Smectymnuus and a tireless labourer in the Assembly that framed the Confession and Catechisms. The dictionary honours Marshall as a preacher who set the word of God before rulers and nations, reminding the judges of the land that they judge not for man, but for the LORD (2Ch 19:6), and who counted the work of reformation a great work from which he would not come down (Neh 6:3). His preaching moved a kingdom, for good and sometimes beyond what later wisdom would approve; yet his aim was the honour of God and the reforming of the church, and he stands among the Westminster divines whose labours gave the Reformed churches their fullest confession of the faith.

A leading preacher of the Long Parliament and a Westminster divine, famed for his sermon Meroz Cursed.

Key Scripture

Jdg 5:23 — "Curse ye Meroz, said the angel of the LORD, curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof; because they came not to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty."

2Ch 19:6 — "And said to the judges, Take heed what ye do: for ye judge not for man, but for the LORD, who is with you in the judgment."

Neh 6:3 — "And I sent messengers unto them, saying, I am doing a great work, so that I cannot come down: why should the work cease, whilst I leave it, and come down to you?"

Hag 1:4 — "Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?"

Modern Corruption

He roused a slumbering people to the cause of reformation and set the word of God before rulers and nations.

expand to see more

The corruption Marshall preached against was the slothful neutrality of those who would not stir for the cause of God, the men of Meroz who came not to the help of the LORD against the mighty. He summoned a slumbering people to the work of reformation, and reminded the rulers of the land that they judge not for man but for the LORD. The dictionary honours this prophetic boldness that set the word of God before the highest powers.

What is honourable in Marshall is the seriousness with which he held the cause of God before a nation. This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that the work of reformation is a great work, not to be left undone while men dwell at ease in their cieled houses. His preaching moved a kingdom, and not in every particular as later wisdom would approve; yet his aim was the honour of God and the reforming of the church, and he laboured faithfully in the Assembly that gave the Reformed churches their fullest confession of the faith.
